title: CDC tracking five active foodborne outbreaks — including oysters distributed in Texas
excerpt: The CDC is tracking five active multistate foodborne outbreaks tied to oysters, raw milk cheese and sprouts, with 168 illnesses reported and recalls in effect — and Texas is among the states where the recalled oysters were sold.
content:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is tracking five active multistate foodborne outbreaks tied to oysters, raw milk cheese and sprouts, together involving 168 reported illnesses and no deaths to date, with recalls in effect for four of them. Texas is among the states where the recalled oysters were distributed — a direct reason for local shoppers and restaurants to check what they have on hand.

The largest new investigation involves Salmonella linked to raw oysters harvested by the Little Wicomico Oyster Company from the Little Wicomico River in Virginia. The CDC's October 19 notice counted 27 cases across 12 states, with 5 hospitalizations; the Virginia Department of Health, counting a wider genomic group, reported 53 people in 18 states. The company voluntarily recalled whole shellstock oysters harvested September 18 through October 8, 2026, identified by shellfish shipper number VA-1421-SP, and Virginia temporarily closed the harvest area. The FDA's safety alert lists Texas among the states where the oysters were distributed, along with California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Maryland, Missouri, North Carolina, New Jersey, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia, plus Washington, D.C.

A second outbreak involves E. coli linked to raw milk cheese: 13 cases in 9 states, 8 hospitalizations, 3 of them involving hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious kidney complication. More than half of those sickened are children aged 5 and younger. Sierra Nevada Cheese Company recalled all Graziers grass-fed raw milk cheeses, including medium cheddar, sharp cheddar, jalapeño jack and Monterey jack, sold in 8-ounce and 16-ounce retail packages and 5-pound food-service loaves.

Recalls are also in effect for alfalfa and radish sprouts and for broccoli sprouts tied to separate investigations. The CDC notes that clinicians may see overlapping symptoms across these outbreaks, so exposure history and reporting to local health departments matter — and the agency's broader table lists 29 active multistate investigations as of October 21, most of which never become public outbreak notices.

What to watch next: updated case counts from the CDC and FDA, whether the oyster investigation converges on a single source beyond the recalled harvest area, and any additional recalls. Anyone with recalled oysters, cheese or sprouts should follow the recall instructions rather than consume them; this story is a news report, not medical advice.

Update — October 30, 2026: Virginia health officials have tied the oyster outbreak's Salmonella strain to more than one harvest site. In an October 26 update reported October 28 by Nature World News, the Virginia Department of Health said whole genome sequencing found Salmonella Telelkebir — the outbreak's serotype — in five isolates from Little Wicomico River oysters, present in each of the four leases sampled. The finding points to a problem in the harvest water rather than a single cage, though officials have not identified a contamination source, according to the report. The river remains closed to oyster and clam harvesting, and Virginia said reopening will require three consecutive rounds of product testing, meaning the closure could outlast its initial 30-day period. The CDC case counts in the original story above have not changed in this update.

Update — October 31, 2026: The CDC's October 30 update raises the oyster outbreak count to 28 illnesses in 13 states — one new case and one new state (Indiana) since the October 19 notice — with five hospitalizations and no deaths, according to the FDA's October 30 safety alert. The CDC now states that oysters harvested by Little Wicomico Oyster Company from the Little Wicomico River made people sick in this outbreak, dropping the earlier wording that they may be making people sick. Illness onset dates now run May 29 to October 6, 2026; the October 6 onset falls inside the September 18 to October 8 harvest window covered by the recall. The Pennsylvania distributor sample that had tested positive for Salmonella turned out to be Salmonella Litchfield, which does not match any sick person, so the laboratory link rests on the Virginia river oysters. The recalled oysters are past shelf life, nothing is being harvested from the river now, and the river remains closed.

Update — November 6, 2026: The sprouts outbreak in this story is now over. In a November 4, 2026 update, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said the Salmonella Bovismorbificans outbreak linked to broccoli sprouts and microgreens is closed: the CDC has declared the outbreak over and the FDA investigation is complete. The outbreak sickened 34 people in six states — Idaho, Minnesota, Montana, Oregon, Utah and Washington — with illnesses from July 7 to September 11, 2026, three hospitalizations and no deaths. Of 30 people interviewed, 29 reported eating sprouts or microgreens. The FDA traced the contamination to a lot of broccoli seed imported from New Zealand; samples of Evergreen Fresh Sprouts-brand broccoli sprouts matched the outbreak strain by whole genome sequencing. All affected sprouts and seeds were recalled, are past expiration and are no longer for sale. This was a separate outbreak from the alfalfa-sprouts E. coli and Salmonella investigation also covered in this story. The oyster outbreak remains open: Virginia health officials said in a November 4 update that the Little Wicomico River harvest area stays closed beyond its initial 30-day emergency closure, and reopening still requires three consecutive rounds of negative product testing; a third round of oyster samples was collected November 2, with results not yet posted.

Update — November 12, 2026

Virginia health officials reported that a third round of oysters taken from Little Wicomico Oyster Company cages on November 2 tested positive for Salmonella — three of eight meat samples from two of the company’s four leases, according to Food Safety News, citing the Virginia Department of Health. A fourth round of samples was collected November 9, with results still pending at the state lab. The Little Wicomico River remains closed to shellfish harvest with no end date under a condemnation order that took effect November 8, and the river cannot reopen until three consecutive rounds of testing come back clean. The CDC count stands at 28 people sick with Salmonella Telelkebir in 13 states, five of them hospitalized and none dead.
